problems.title: Bytes in flight on a datacenter GPU
problems.statement: A GPU has 3.35 TB/s of DRAM bandwidth and a loaded memory latency of 600 ns.

parts.prompt: How many bytes must be in flight to sustain full bandwidth?
How many 4-byte loads is that?

hints: Little's law: in flight = throughput × latency. Keep the units straight: TB/s × ns.
problems.solution:
$L = \lambda W = 3.35\times10^{12}\,\tfrac{\text{B}}{\text{s}} \times 600\times10^{-9}\,\text{s} = 2,010,000$ bytes ≈ 2 MB.

(b) At 4 bytes per load: $502,500$ loads in flight. Half a million independent loads, at every moment: no small set of cores can do that.

problems.title: One outstanding miss
problems.statement: A single CPU thread walks a linked list. Each node lives in a different 64-byte cache line, every access misses to DRAM, and DRAM latency is 80 ns. The next address isn't known until the current load returns.

parts.prompt: What bandwidth does the thread achieve?
What fraction of a 50 GB/s memory system is that, in %?

hints: How many requests can be in flight when each address depends on the previous load?
λ = L / W with L = one 64-byte line.
problems.solution:
Each load depends on the previous one, so exactly one request is in flight: $L = 64$ bytes. Little's law gives $\lambda = L/W = 64\,\text{B} / 80\,\text{ns} = 0.8$ GB/s (bytes per ns = GB/s).

(b) $0.8/50 = 1.6\%$. Pointer chasing is latency-bound: more bandwidth wouldn't help at all, only lower latency would.

problems.title: Cycles, nanoseconds and bytes
problems.statement: A GPU's memory latency is quoted as 400 cycles at a 1.8 GHz clock. Its bandwidth is 1 TB/s.

parts.prompt: Latency in nanoseconds?
Bytes in flight to sustain full bandwidth?

hints: One cycle at 1.8 GHz lasts 1/1.8 ns.
problems.solution:
(a) $400 / 1.8\,\text{GHz} = 222.2$ ns.

(b) $1000\,\text{GB/s} \times 222.22\,\text{ns} = 222,222$ bytes. Mixing cycles and seconds is the most common slip in these calculations: convert once, at the start.

problems.title: Threads with several loads each
problems.statement: Bandwidth is 900 GB/s and loaded latency 500 ns. Each thread issues 4 independent 4-byte loads before it needs any of the results, and keeps them all in flight.

parts.prompt: Bytes in flight needed?
Minimum number of threads to saturate the memory?
And if each thread kept only one load in flight?

hints: Each thread contributes 4 × 4 = 16 bytes in flight.
Threads must be a whole number, and enough: round up.
problems.solution:
(a) $900 \times 500 = 450,000$ bytes.

(b) Each thread holds $4 \times 4 = 16$ bytes in flight, so $\lceil 450,000 / 16 \rceil = 28,125$ threads.

(c) $\lceil 450,000/4 \rceil = 112,500$. Four independent loads per thread (instruction-level parallelism) substitute for four times as many threads (thread-level parallelism). Chapter 0.3 and Volkov's paper (Part 2) come back to this trade.

problems.title: A machine with fixed concurrency
problems.statement: An accelerator can track at most 64,000 bytes of outstanding reads. Its memory has 300 ns latency and a peak of 400 GB/s.

parts.prompt: What bandwidth can it actually reach?
What percentage of peak is that?
How many bytes of tracking would it need to reach peak?

hints: Throughput is the smaller of two limits: the peak, and what the concurrency allows.
problems.solution:
Achieved bandwidth is bounded by both the peak and Little's law: $\lambda = \min(P, L/W) = \min(400, 64000/300) = \min(400, 213.3) = 213.3$ GB/s, i.e. $53.3\%$ of peak.

(c) To reach peak it would need $L = P W = 400 \times 300 = 120,000$ bytes. Hardware designers size miss-tracking structures (MSHRs on CPUs) exactly this way.

problems.title: Why one CPU core can't saturate memory
problems.statement: A CPU core can track 10 outstanding L1 misses (each a 64-byte line). DRAM latency is 90 ns. The memory system delivers 200 GB/s.

parts.prompt: Maximum bandwidth one core can draw?
Minimum number of cores to saturate the memory system?

hints: Little's law per core: λ = (10 × 64 B) / 90 ns.
problems.solution:
(a) $\lambda = 640\,\text{B} / 90\,\text{ns} = 7.11$ GB/s.

(b) $\lceil 200 / 7.111 \rceil = 29$ cores. This is why memory-bound CPU code needs many cores, and why hardware prefetchers (which add requests in flight) matter so much on CPUs.

problems.title: Little's law outside computers
problems.statement: A web service handles a steady 2,000 requests per second, and each request spends on average 15 ms in the service.

parts.prompt: On average, how many requests are inside the service at once?
Which assumption does Little's law need?
options: A steady state: on average, requests leave as fast as they arrive

problems.solution:
(a) $L = \lambda W = 2000\,\text{s}^{-1} \times 0.015\,\text{s} = 30$ requests.

(b) Little's law holds for averages in any system in steady state, whatever the arrival distribution, ordering or variation in latency. That generality is why it's the first tool to reach for.

problems.title: Latency that rises with load
problems.statement: Latency isn't constant: as a memory system gets busier, requests queue. Model the loaded latency as $W(\lambda) = W_0 / (1 - \lambda / P)$, with idle latency $W_0 = 270$ ns and peak $P = 512$ GB/s. A program keeps exactly 100,000 bytes in flight at all times.

parts.prompt: If latency stayed at 270 ns, what bandwidth would Little's law predict?
What bandwidth does it actually reach, with the loaded latency?
What is the loaded latency at that bandwidth?

hints: The bandwidth λ and the latency W(λ) depend on each other: λ = L / W(λ). Solve for λ.
λ = L(1 − λ/P) / W₀. Collect the λ terms.
problems.solution:
(a) $100000 / 270 = 370.4$ GB/s.

(b) Little's law must hold at the operating point: $\lambda = L / W(\lambda) = \frac{L}{W_0}\left(1 - \frac{\lambda}{P}\right)$. So $\lambda\left(1 + \frac{L}{W_0 P}\right) = \frac{L}{W_0}$, giving $\lambda = \frac{L/W_0}{1 + L/(W_0 P)} = \frac{370.4}{1 + 0.723} = 214.9$ GB/s.

(c) $W = 270 / (1 - 214.9/512) = 465.3$ ns. Queueing raised the latency, which lowered the throughput the same concurrency buys. Always use loaded latency in Little's law; the idle number overestimates what you'll get.

problems.title: Sizing ILP for a GPU
problems.statement: A GPU has 80 SMs, each holding 48 resident warps. A warp-wide load of 4-byte values moves 128 bytes. Memory: 2 TB/s, 500 ns loaded latency.

parts.prompt: Bytes in flight if every warp has exactly one load outstanding?
Bytes in flight needed for full bandwidth?
Minimum independent loads each warp must keep in flight (a whole number)?
With one load per warp, what percentage of peak bandwidth can you reach?

hints: Count the machine's concurrency: SMs × warps × bytes per warp request.
If concurrency falls short of the requirement, achieved bandwidth = concurrency / latency.
problems.solution:
(a) $80 \times 48 \times 128 = 491,520$ bytes.

(b) $2000\,\text{GB/s} \times 500\,\text{ns} = 1,000,000$ bytes.

(c) $\lceil 1,000,000 / 491,520 \rceil = \lceil 2.03 \rceil = 3$ independent loads per warp.

(d) $491,520 / 1,000,000 = 49.2\%$. Even a huge GPU fully occupied falls short with one load per warp: real kernels issue several loads (often as vector loads) before using them.

problems.title: Requests of different sizes
problems.statement: On the GW-1 (512 GB/s, 270 ns), half of a kernel's memory requests are 128 bytes and half are 32 bytes.

parts.prompt: Bytes in flight needed for full bandwidth?
Average request size?
Requests in flight needed?

hints: Little's law also holds for requests: requests in flight = bytes in flight / mean bytes per request.
problems.solution: (a) $512 \times 270 = 138,240$ bytes. (b) Mean size $= 0.5(128) + 0.5(32) = 80$ bytes. (c) $138,240 / 80 = 1,728$ requests. Small requests are expensive: they need more of them in flight for the same bytes, which is one reason GPUs work hard to combine lanes' accesses into wide transactions (coalescing, Part 2).
